Controlling Network Traffic

sections.title: FIREWALLS & TRAFFIC
sections.subtitle: Slide 2 of 13 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
Why Control Traffic In and Out?

You only want traffic to enter or leave your server that actually needs to. A firewall lets you control inbound (ingress) and outbound (egress) traffic — the same least-privilege principle you'd apply to IAM permissions.

Open only what's needed

A web server usually needs just port 80 (HTTP) and 443 (HTTPS) open. Everything else stays closed.

Fewer holes, less risk

A strict firewall shuts down a lot of possible security holes before they become a problem.

Prevent accidents too

Not opening outbound SMTP on a test system stops it from accidentally emailing real customers.

Firewalls & Traffic

2

sections.title: FIREWALLS & TRAFFIC
sections.subtitle: Slide 3 of 13 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
Inbound vs. Outbound Traffic

Inbound (Ingress)

Traffic coming into your server from somewhere else — like a visitor's browser requesting your website.

Outbound (Egress)

Traffic leaving your server — like your server calling out to an API, sending mail, or pulling updates.

Before traffic can enter or leave your instance, it passes through a firewall that inspects it and applies your rules.

Firewalls & Traffic

3

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

sections.title: FIREWALLS & TRAFFIC
sections.subtitle: Slide 4 of 13 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
How a Request Travels Through the Firewall

Source

10.0.0.10

Firewall

Rules

Allow

Deny

Inspects traffic and filters it based on your rules

Destination

10.10.0.20

inbound

outbound response

EXAMPLE REQUEST

SSH (TCP, port 22) from 10.0.0.10 → 10.10.0.20

The firewall checks its rules — if a rule allows TCP:22 from this source to this destination, the request passes through.

THE THREE STEPS

1. Source sends the request  ·  2. Firewall checks its rules  ·  3. If allowed, destination receives it and can respond

Firewalls & Traffic

sections.title: SECURITY GROUPS
sections.subtitle: Slide 5 of 13 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
The Default Behavior

Inbound: Denied by default

Nothing can reach your server until you explicitly add a rule allowing it in.

Outbound: Allowed by default

Your server can reach out anywhere — until the moment you add your first outbound rule.

The switch to watch for

The moment you add any outbound rule, the default flips from “allow all” to “deny all” — only the exceptions you've explicitly added stay allowed.

Security Groups

5

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

sections.title: SECURITY GROUPS
sections.subtitle: Slide 6 of 13 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
What a Security Group Rule Can Match

A security group is a set of rules attached to your AWS resources (like EC2 instances). Each rule can filter on:

Direction

Inbound or outbound

IP Protocol

TCP, UDP, or ICMP

Source / Destination IP

A specific address or CIDR range

Port

e.g. 22 for SSH, 443 for HTTPS

Source / Dest. Security Group

Another security group, not just an IP (AWS-only)

Good practice: define rules as restrictive as possible. AWS won't stop you from allowing everything — but you should.

Security Groups

6

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

sections.title: SECURITY GROUPS
sections.subtitle: Slide 7 of 13 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
Source vs. Destination: Which Way Rules Filter

Inbound rules filter by SOURCE

Where is this traffic coming from? You allow inbound traffic only from specific source IP ranges — or specific security groups.

Outbound rules filter by DESTINATION

Where is this traffic going? You allow outbound traffic only to specific destination IP ranges — or specific security groups.

AWS is responsible for the firewall itself — you're responsible for the rules you write.

Security Groups

7

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

sections.title: SECURITY GROUPS
sections.subtitle: Slide 8 of 13 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
Why Reference a Security Group Instead of an IP?

Cloud servers come and go — rules based on fixed source IP addresses get out of date fast. Referencing a security group instead stays correct automatically.

EXAMPLE

MySQL database

only accessible from

Web servers

(a security group, not a fixed IP)

Web servers

only accessible from

Web cache servers

As you add or remove web servers, both rules stay correct automatically — no manual IP list to maintain.

Security Groups

8

sections.title: BASTION HOST PATTERN
sections.subtitle: Slide 9 of 13 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
The Problem: Too Many Doors

If every server allows SSH directly from the internet, you have many possible entry points to defend — and if any one server is compromised, an attacker may be able to jump to the others.

The fix: a bastion host (sometimes called a “jump box”)

Only one server — the bastion host — can be reached via SSH from the internet, ideally restricted to a specific source IP. Every other server can only be reached via SSH from the bastion host itself.

Bastion Host Pattern

9

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

sections.title: BASTION HOST PATTERN
sections.subtitle: Slide 10 of 13 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
Implementing It: Two Rules

1

Allow SSH to the bastion host

From 0.0.0.0/0, or better, a specific known source IP address.

2

Allow SSH to every other server — but only from the bastion

The source for this rule is the bastion host's security group, not the open internet.

Bastion Host Pattern

10

sections.title: BASTION HOST PATTERN
sections.subtitle: Slide 12 of 13 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
Why This Pattern Works

One entry point, one job

You have a single entry point into your system, and that entry point does nothing but SSH. The chances of it being compromised are small.

No lateral movement

If a web server, mail server, or FTP server is hacked, the attacker can't jump from that server to all the others.

Bastion Host Pattern

12

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.subtitle: Slide 13 of 13 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
Open only the ports you need — typically 80/443 for a web server — and close everything else.

Inbound traffic is denied by default; outbound is allowed by default until you add a rule.

Reference security groups instead of fixed IPs so rules stay correct as servers change.

A bastion host gives you one controlled entry point and stops attackers from moving laterally.

Virtual Private Cloud

Designing a private network in the cloud — subnets, route tables, ACLs, and gateways

01

VPC Fundamentals

02

Example Architecture

03

Network ACLs

04

Extending the Pattern

Overview

1

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

sections.title: VPC FUNDAMENTALS
sections.subtitle: Slide 2 of 13 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
What Is a Virtual Private Cloud?

A VPC gives you your own private network in the cloud. “Private” means you use reserved address ranges that aren't necessarily connected to the public internet — you decide what connects out and what stays isolated.

PRIVATE ADDRESS RANGES YOU CAN USE

10.0.0.0/8

16.7 million addresses — the most common choice for large networks

172.16.0.0/12

1 million addresses — a mid-sized private range

192.168.0.0/16

65,536 addresses — familiar from home routers

VPC Fundamentals

2

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

sections.title: VPC FUNDAMENTALS
sections.subtitle: Slide 3 of 13 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
The Building Blocks of a VPC

Subnets

Slices of your network address space where you place resources.

Route Tables

Rules that decide where traffic from a subnet is allowed to go.

Access Control Lists

Firewall-like rules that filter traffic between subnets.

Gateways

Controlled doors to the internet or to a VPN connection.

A subnet lets you separate concerns — a new subnet for your databases, web servers, caches, or app servers, wherever you need to isolate one system from another.

VPC Fundamentals

3

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

sections.title: VPC FUNDAMENTALS
sections.subtitle: Slide 4 of 13 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
Public vs. Private Subnets: The Rule of Thumb

At minimum, plan for two kinds of subnets:

Public Subnet

Has a route to the internet

Anything that needs to be reachable from outside — typically your web servers or load balancers — belongs here.

Private Subnet

No route to the internet

Anything that should never be reachable directly — typically your databases — belongs here, safely out of reach.

VPC Fundamentals

4

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

sections.title: WORKED EXAMPLE
sections.subtitle: Slide 5 of 13 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
Hosting an Enterprise Web App

You'll design a VPC that keeps the web servers safely out of direct reach, fronts them with a cache, and gives admins a single, controlled way in.

Bastion host

The only way in for SSH admin access

Web cache

Absorbs traffic and shields the web servers

Web servers

Never directly reachable from the internet

sections.title: NETWORK ACLS
sections.subtitle: Slide 8 of 13 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
Network ACLs: A Firewall Between Subnets

A network ACL restricts traffic moving from one subnet to another — like a firewall placed at each subnet's border. Each rule names a source, a destination, and what's allowed through.

Source

Where the traffic comes from — a CIDR range or another subnet.

Protocol / Port

What kind of traffic — e.g. SSH (22) or HTTP (80).

Destination

Which subnet the traffic is allowed to reach.

Network ACLs

8

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

sections.title: NETWORK ACLS
sections.subtitle: Slide 9 of 13 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
ACL Rules: SSH Access (the Bastion Pattern)

SSH is allowed to flow in one controlled direction — through the bastion host only:

0.0.0.0/0

→  SSH  →

10.0.1.0/24

Anyone on the internet can reach the bastion host over SSH.

10.0.1.0/24

→  SSH  →

10.0.2.0/24

The bastion can SSH into the Varnish cache subnet.

10.0.1.0/24

→  SSH  →

10.0.3.0/24

The bastion can SSH into the Apache web server subnet.

Network ACLs

9

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

sections.title: NETWORK ACLS
sections.subtitle: Slide 10 of 13 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
ACL Rules: HTTP Access (the Caching Pattern)

HTTP traffic flows from the public internet, through the cache, to the web server — never directly:

0.0.0.0/0

→  HTTP  →

10.0.2.0/24

Anyone on the internet can reach the Varnish web cache over HTTP.

10.0.2.0/24

→  HTTP  →

10.0.3.0/24

The cache can forward HTTP requests to the Apache web servers.

What's NOT allowed

There is no rule allowing 0.0.0.0/0 → 10.0.3.0/24. The web servers can never be reached directly from the internet — only through the cache.

Network ACLs

10

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

sections.title: NETWORK ACLS
sections.subtitle: Slide 11 of 13 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
Two Journeys Through the Network

A Website Visitor

1

Requests the page over HTTP

2

Hits the Internet Gateway

3

Reaches the Varnish cache (public)

4

Cache serves it directly, or forwards to Apache (private)

5

Apache never sees the internet directly

An Administrator

1

Connects over SSH

2

Hits the Internet Gateway

3

Reaches the bastion host (public)

4

Bastion relays SSH to the cache or Apache subnet

5

No other path into those private servers exists

Network ACLs

11

sections.title: EXTENDING THE PATTERN
sections.subtitle: Slide 12 of 13 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
NAT & VPN Gateways

Real enterprise networks often add two more pieces:

Private VPC · 10.10.0.0/16

Internet

Corporate network

Public subnet

NAT gateway

VPN gateway

Private subnet

App server

Private subnet

Database

NAT gateway

Lets private servers reach out to the internet (e.g. for updates) without accepting inbound connections.

VPN gateway

Extends your office network directly into the VPC, so private resources are reachable without going over the public internet.

Extending the Pattern

12

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

![Slide Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.subtitle: Slide 13 of 13 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
A VPC is your own private network, built from reserved address ranges you fully control.

Subnets let you isolate concerns — keep at least a public and a private subnet for every tier.

A bastion host and a cache tier mean nothing sensitive is ever reachable directly from the internet.

Network ACLs enforce exactly which traffic can move between subnets — nothing more.

Summary

sections.title: HIGH AVAILABILITY ON AWS
sections.subtitle: Slide 1 of 9 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
* 
Recovery

* Keeping a virtual server running — and what happens to its data — when an entire availability zone goes down.

sections.title: THE BASICS
sections.subtitle: Slide 2 of 9 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
* What Auto-Scaling Does
* Multiple subnets
* Auto-scaling can start EC2 instances across several subnets, not just one.
* Automatic failover
* If an entire availability zone has an outage, a new virtual server can be launched into another subnet in another zone.
* Continuous monitoring
* Auto-scaling watches the health of running servers and reacts when something goes wrong.
* AUTO-SCALING & MULTI-AZ RECOVERY
* 2

sections.title: SETTING IT UP
sections.subtitle: Slide 3 of 9 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
* Launch Configuration
* Everything needed to launch a single virtual server:
* Image (AMI) to start the new server from
* Instance type — the size of the virtual server
* Auto-Scaling Group
* Tells EC2 how many servers to run and where:
* Min / max / desired number of virtual servers
* Health check for the virtual servers
* Subnets to launch virtual servers in
* AUTO-SCALING & MULTI-AZ RECOVERY
* 3

sections.title: PUTTING IT TOGETHER
sections.subtitle: Slide 4 of 9 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
* 
• Health check for virtual servers
• Subnets to launch virtual servers in

* 
• Size of virtual server

* 
virtual servers

* How Auto-Scaling Reacts to a Failure
* Auto-scaling group
* Launch configuration
* 2. If there aren't enough healthy virtual servers, new ones are launched based on the launch configuration.
* AUTO-SCALING & MULTI-AZ RECOVERY
* 4

sections.title: TWO DIFFERENT RECOVERY MECHANISMS
sections.subtitle: Slide 5 of 9 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
* CloudWatch Alarm Recovery
* Launches an identical copy of the original virtual server if it fails — but only in the same availability zone.
* Why only the same zone?
* The private IP address and the EBS volume of a virtual server are bound to a single subnet and a single availability zone.
* Auto-Scaling Failover
* Can recover a failed virtual server into a completely different availability zone — true protection against a data center outage.
* Example: a Jenkins CI server
* If a team relies on Jenkins to test, build, and deploy software, auto-scaling lets it fail over into another zone instead of staying down during a data center outage.
* AUTO-SCALING & MULTI-AZ RECOVERY
* 5

sections.title: READ BEFORE YOU RELY ON AUTO-SCALING
sections.subtitle: Slide 6 of 9 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
* Pitfall: Network-Attached Storage
* Availability zone A
* Virtual server
* EBS volume
* EBS volume is bound to availability zone A
* Availability zone B
* Virtual server
* EBS volume
* New and empty EBS volume
* Launch new virtual server in other availability zone
* AUTO-SCALING & MULTI-AZ RECOVERY
* 6

sections.title: FIXING THE PITFALL
sections.subtitle: Slide 7 of 9 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
* Three Ways to Recover Your Data
* 1
* Use a multi-AZ managed service
* 2
* Use EBS snapshots
* Snapshot your EBS volumes and restore from the snapshot when a server recovers in another zone. Snapshots are stored on S3, so they're available across zones.
* 3
* Use distributed third-party storage
* Tools like GlusterFS, DRBD, or MongoDB replicate data across zones themselves — powerful, but adds real operational complexity.
* AUTO-SCALING & MULTI-AZ RECOVERY
* 7

sections.title: WORKED EXAMPLE
sections.subtitle: Slide 8 of 9 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
* Choosing a Recovery Strategy for Jenkins
* 1
* The constraint
* 2
* Why plain EBS isn't enough
* An EBS volume only exists in a single availability zone, which is exactly the problem being solved — so it can't be the whole answer.
* 3
* Why skip distributed storage
* GlusterFS, DRBD, and similar tools would work, but they introduce a level of operational complexity that isn't justified here.
* 4
* The chosen solution: EBS snapshots
* Recover the virtual server in another availability zone using an EBS snapshot. You only lose the data written since the last snapshot — not the entire volume.
* AUTO-SCALING & MULTI-AZ RECOVERY
* 8

sections.title: KEY TAKEAWAYS
sections.subtitle: Slide 9 of 9 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
* Auto-scaling needs two pieces: a launch configuration (what to launch) and an auto-scaling group (how many, where, and how to monitor).
* A CloudWatch alarm can only recover a server in the same availability zone; auto-scaling can fail it over into a different zone entirely.
* EBS volumes are bound to a single availability zone — they don't automatically follow a server that recovers elsewhere.
* Fix that gap with a multi-AZ managed service, EBS snapshots, or distributed third-party storage — pick based on what your app actually needs.
* For disk-based apps like Jenkins, EBS snapshots hit the sweet spot: real recovery, without the complexity of distributed storage.
* AUTO-SCALING & MULTI-AZ RECOVERY
* 9

* Tools like GlusterFS, DRBD, or MongoDB replicate data across zones themselves — powerful, but adds real operational complexity.
* AUTO-SCALING & MULTI-AZ RECOVERY

sections.subtitle: Slide 8 of 9 • PowerPoint Deck

* Choosing a Recovery Strategy for Jenkins
* 1
* The constraint
* 2
* Why plain EBS isn't enough
* An EBS volume only exists in a single availability zone, which is exactly the problem being solved — so it can't be the whole answer.
* 3
* Why skip distributed storage
* GlusterFS, DRBD, and similar tools would work, but they introduce a level of operational complexity that isn't justified here.
* 4
* The chosen solution: EBS snapshots
* Recover the virtual server in another availability zone using an EBS snapshot. You only lose the data written since the last snapshot — not the entire volume.
* AUTO-SCALING & MULTI-AZ RECOVERY
* 8

sections.title: KEY TAKEAWAYS
sections.subtitle: Slide 9 of 9 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
* Auto-scaling needs two pieces: a launch configuration (what to launch) and an auto-scaling group (how many, where, and how to monitor).
* A CloudWatch alarm can only recover a server in the same availability zone; auto-scaling can fail it over into a different zone entirely.
* EBS volumes are bound to a single availability zone — they don't automatically follow a server that recovers elsewhere.
* Fix that gap with a multi-AZ managed service, EBS snapshots, or distributed third-party storage — pick based on what your app actually needs.
* For disk-based apps like Jenkins, EBS snapshots hit the sweet spot: real recovery, without the complexity of distributed storage.
